The Doian culture, or the Doian industry, is a Late Stone Age (Upper Paleolithic ) archaeological culture and stone tool industry found in the southern and central regions of the Somali Peninsula, primarily in present-day southern Somalia . The term "Doian" was coined by the British archaeologist J. Desmond Clark to describe a cohesive series of Late Stone Age industries that emerged from the earlier Somaliland Magosian  through transitional stages. The name derives from the southern Somali word doi, which refers to the flat, scrub-covered, red-sand plains typical of southern Somalia, where many Doian factory and habitation sites have been discovered. In the 1930s, Italian archaeologist Paolo Graziosi conducted one of the first archaeological investigations in Somalia, focusing especially on the southern part of the country. He identified a Late Stone Age industry, which he initially referred to as “Eibian,” named after the Buur Heybe site where the material was primarily found. J. Desmond Clark introduced the term “Doian” before Graziosi’s reports were published. Graziosi had suggested “Eibian” for the industry at Buur Heybe, but Clark rejected this narrower designation in favor of a broader term that could encompass the full range of related Late Stone Age industries across southern Somalia.
The Doian industry is characterized by advanced microliths, arrowheads, pressure-flaked points, scrapers, small backed blades, and various other types of stone tools used for hunting, food processing, and other subsistence activities. The Doian hunter-gatherer communities practiced a foraging lifestyle, exploiting diverse environments across southern and central Somalia, including the southern Haud (Ciid region), parts of the Ogaden (today’s Somali region in Ethiopia), and possibly as far as Trans-Jubba (between the Jubba and Tana river). Its distribution may have also included the southern part of Puntland (northern Mudug, administered by Puntland) and the Danakil Rift.
In the 1980s, the American archaeologist Steven Brandt conducted excavations at the large Buur Heybe inselberg, studying its two rockshelters, Gogoshiis Qabe and Guli Waabayo, under the Buur Ecological and Archaeological Project (BEAP). These investigations revealed a later industry at Buur Heybe, which Brandt termed the Bardaale industry, named after a nearby settlement. The Bardaale industry succeeded and replaced the earlier Eibian (Doian) tradition and is believed to have developed after the end of the Late Pleistocene, emerging in the early Holocene. The transition from Doian to Bardaale at Buur Heybe appears to have occurred during a period of major environmental change near the end of Marine Isotope Stage 2 (MIS 2). While the Bardaale represents an early Neolithic onset, the Doian marks the final transition from Middle Stone Age to Late Stone Age technologies in southern and central Somalia, reflecting increasing regional specialization and technological sophistication prior to the Neolithic.
Distribution
The Doian culture is concentrated on the southern plateau and coastal plain of Somalia, particularly between the Webi Shebeli and Juba rivers. It is also represented in the southern Haud, although its presence diminishes rapidly toward the north. No typical Doian tools have been identified within Somaliland, and only a few mixed sites exist in the southern Puntland. While detailed archaeological work has yet to be carried out in eastern Banaadir or Trans-Jubaland (between the Juba and Tana rivers), it is believed that Doian sites likely occur there. To the west, the Doian extends into the Ogaden, although in these northern and western regions it appears to be replaced by regional variants of the Wilton industry. A possible Doian-related industry may exist in the Danakil Rift, although evidence is limited and may reflect a Magosian–Wilton developmental sequence.
Material culture
The Doian culture is characterized by a high degree of technical sophistication for the Late Stone Age. Its most distinctive tools include:
* Pressure-flaked points – finely retouched spear or arrow points
* Hollow-based arrowheads – a distinctive form of arrow tip
* Small backed blades – elongated blades with a blunted edge
* Microlithic bladelets – small, sharp blades used in composite tools
* Retouched scrapers – for processing hides, wood, and plant materials
* Geometric microliths – small trapezoids, triangles, and crescents for composite tools
These tools indicate strong regional specialization and early tendencies toward Neolithic-style craftsmanship, such as standardized forms and advanced pressure-flaking techniques. While the Doian industry is a direct derivative of the Somaliland Magosian, certain elements, notably hollow-based arrowheads and highly regular microliths, suggest external influences, possibly introduced from the Harar plateau and the southeastern Sahara.
Key sites
The most important Doian sites include Buur heybe, notably the Gure Warbei, and the Rifle Range site at Buur Hakaba. Excavations at these locations provide the primary evidence for defining the Doian cultural complex. Additional coastal sites show variations, such as strand-looping forms or tools exhibiting more pronounced "neolithic" characteristics, though these do not imply fully Neolithic lifestyles, such as permanent settlements or domestication of animals beyond dogs.
